concepts.name: Classification of Public Debt: Internal vs External — Definitional Boundaries
key_dimensions: Residency-based vs currency-based classification: why a rupee-denominated bond held by a foreign investor is 'external' by one definition but 'internal' by another
IMF/World Bank definition vs RBI/Ministry of Finance definition — where they diverge
UPSC trap: Masala bonds classified as external debt despite being rupee-denominated
Implications of misclassification for currency risk and sovereign vulnerability assessments

concepts.name: Constitutional Provisions Governing Public Borrowing: Articles 292, 293, and 246
key_dimensions: Article 292: Union's power to borrow on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India — no ceiling specified in Constitution
Article 293: States can only borrow within India; cannot borrow externally without Centre's consent
UPSC trap: States need Centre's consent for external borrowing — absolute restriction, not conditional
Seventh Schedule Entry 35 (Union List) vs Entry 43 (State List) — borrowing powers demarcation
Parliament sets limits via the annual Finance Bill — not a permanent statutory cap

concepts.name: Instruments of Internal Public Debt: G-Secs, T-Bills, CMBs, and SDL
key_dimensions: Distinction between dated government securities (G-Secs, >1 year) and Treasury Bills (91, 182, 364 days)
Cash Management Bills (CMBs): sub-91-day instruments, not part of the regular borrowing calendar — UPSC trap
State Development Loans (SDLs): issued by states through RBI, carry a spread over central G-Secs
Ways and Means Advances (WMA) vs Market Borrowings — WMA is temporary overdraft, NOT public debt
Sovereign Gold Bonds as a hybrid internal debt instrument — how they differ from conventional G-Secs

concepts.name: External Debt Composition and Creditor Categories
key_dimensions: Multilateral debt (World Bank, ADB, IMF) vs Bilateral debt vs Commercial borrowings — risk profiles differ
NRI deposits (FCNR-B, NRE accounts) counted as external debt — often missed in UPSC answers
External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs): automatic vs approval route, end-use restrictions
Masala bonds, FPI holdings in G-Secs, and Sovereign bonds — newer categories in India's external debt
Concessional vs non-concessional external debt — significance for debt sustainability

concepts.name: Debt-to-GDP Ratio: Measurement, India's Trajectory, and FRBM Targets
key_dimensions: FRBM Act 2003 original targets vs NK Singh Committee (2017) revised recommendation: 60% of GDP (Centre 40% + States 20%)
India's general government debt (~83-85% of GDP) vs Central government debt alone (~57-58%) — UPSC frequently tests this distinction
Why India's high debt-to-GDP is considered less dangerous than similar ratios in emerging markets: domestic ownership, long maturity profile
UPSC trap: FRBM targets are for Central government only, not general government (Centre + States)
COVID-19 escape clause invoked under FRBM — fiscal deficit target breach and its legal basis

concepts.name: FRBM Act 2003: Fiscal Consolidation Framework and Its Evolution
key_dimensions: Original targets: fiscal deficit 3% of GDP, revenue deficit 0% — revenue deficit elimination was later dropped
Escape clause (Section 4(3)): allows 0.5% deviation in case of national security, calamity, far-reaching structural reforms
NK Singh Committee recommendations (2017): shift from fiscal deficit target to debt-to-GDP as the primary anchor
Medium-term fiscal policy statement, fiscal policy strategy statement — mandatory documents under FRBM
UPSC trap: FRBM does NOT apply to states directly — states have their own FRBMs modeled on central law

concepts.name: Debt Servicing: Interest Payments, Rollover Risk, and Revenue Implications
key_dimensions: Interest payments as percentage of revenue receipts (debt servicing ratio) — a more revealing metric than debt-to-GDP
Rollover risk: when short-term debt matures faster than repayment capacity — relevance to T-Bill vs G-Sec composition
India's interest-to-revenue-receipts ratio (~40% for Centre) — among the highest in emerging markets
Distinction between capital account (principal repayment) and revenue account (interest payment) in Union Budget
Crowding-out effect: high debt service obligations reducing fiscal space for capital expenditure

concepts.name: Monetisation of Deficit: Ways and Means Advances vs Direct Monetisation
key_dimensions: Historic ad hoc Treasury Bills (pre-1997): automatic monetisation of deficit by RBI — phased out by Rangarajan-Manmohan agreement
WMA (Ways and Means Advances): RBI provides short-term credit to Centre/States against securities — not money creation
Overdraft limits for states under WMA facility — states can be cut off from financial markets if limits breached
COVID-era 'Held to Maturity' relaxation for banks — indirect monetisation through regulatory accommodation
UPSC trap: current framework prohibits RBI from directly subscribing to primary issuance of G-Secs (no direct monetisation)

concepts.name: External Debt Sustainability Indicators: Key Ratios and India's Vulnerability Assessment
key_dimensions: Debt-service ratio = (principal + interest payments) / current account receipts — IMF benchmark <20%
External debt to GNI ratio, short-term debt to total external debt, short-term debt to forex reserves
India's external debt profile: ~$620-640 billion; long-term dominates (~80%); concessional component shrinking
UPSC trap: India is classified as a 'low risk' external debtor by IMF despite high general government debt — because external debt is manageable
Forex reserves to external debt cover ratio — India's buffer and its adequacy during currency stress

concepts.name: Sovereign Credit Rating: Determinants, India's Rating, and the Bias Controversy
key_dimensions: Big Three agencies: Moody's, S&P, Fitch — India rated BBB-/Baa3 (lowest investment grade) for over a decade
Key determinants: debt-to-GDP, fiscal deficit, GDP growth, governance indicators, forex reserves
India's criticism of 'opaque methodology' and alleged bias: high debt-to-GDP but strong growth not adequately rewarded
Consequences of sovereign downgrade: higher borrowing costs, capital outflows, currency depreciation
UPSC trap: sovereign rating affects not just government borrowing but also the ceiling rating for Indian corporates (sovereign ceiling doctrine)

concepts.name: Primary Deficit vs Fiscal Deficit vs Revenue Deficit: Conceptual Distinctions and Policy Signals
key_dimensions: Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts) — financed entirely by borrowing
Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments — measures current policy stance excluding past debt burden
Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts — signals consumption out of borrowed funds
Effective Revenue Deficit (introduced 2011-12): Revenue Deficit minus grants for capital asset creation — UPSC-specific concept
UPSC trap: a zero primary deficit does NOT mean zero fiscal deficit — interest payments still create a gap

concepts.name: Crowding Out Effect: Mechanism, Evidence for India, and Counter-arguments
key_dimensions: Mechanism: government borrowing raises interest rates → private investment becomes costlier → falls
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): mandates banks to hold G-Secs — a structural form of financial repression that facilitates crowding out
Counter-argument (Ricardian Equivalence): rational agents anticipate future taxes, increase savings, offsetting the crowding-out
Empirical evidence for India: mixed — crowding out more evident during high inflation periods
UPSC trap: crowding out is less severe when RBI is accommodative (low repo rate environment) — monetary-fiscal interaction

concepts.name: Debt Management: Role of RBI vs Proposed Debt Management Office (DMO)
key_dimensions: Current arrangement: RBI manages government debt — creates conflict of interest between monetary policy (tight) and debt management (cheap borrowing)
FRBM Review Committee 2017 and multiple committees recommended an independent Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA)
Why India hasn't established PDMA yet: turf issues, concerns about RBI losing G-Sec market influence, coordination challenges
UPSC trap: RBI's debt management role is statutory (RBI Act), not constitutional — can be changed by Parliament
International comparison: UK's DMO, US Treasury's Office of Debt Management — models for India

concepts.name: External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs): Framework, End-Use Restrictions, and Macroprudential Concerns
key_dimensions: ECBs governed by FEMA — automatic route (up to certain limits) vs RBI approval route
End-use restrictions: cannot be used for real estate, equity markets, on-lending for speculative purposes
All-in-cost ceiling: limits total interest and fees to prevent expensive borrowing — periodically revised by RBI
ECB as part of India's capital account management — balance between attracting foreign capital and managing currency/rollover risk
UPSC trap: ECBs are private corporate borrowings abroad but counted in India's external debt — governments don't directly borrow via ECB route

concepts.name: Contingent Liabilities and Off-Balance Sheet Government Obligations
key_dimensions: Explicit contingent liabilities: guarantees given by government to PSU borrowings, state-guaranteed bonds — not in fiscal deficit but risky
Implicit contingent liabilities: bailout of PSBs (recapitalisation bonds), UDAY scheme bonds — politically committed but not legally binding
UPSC trap: Recapitalisation bonds issued to banks are NOT counted in fiscal deficit if structured as below-the-line transactions — debate on accounting treatment
Off-budget borrowings (NSSF loans to FCI, NABARD borrowings): controversy around their exclusion from headline fiscal deficit
CAG's role in flagging contingent liabilities — significance for true fiscal transparency

concepts.name: National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) as a Source of Internal Borrowing
key_dimensions: NSSF pools small savings (PPF, NSC, Kisan Vikas Patra) and lends to Central and State governments
NSSF loans to states historically used to circumvent fiscal deficit limits — bypasses market discipline
Interest rate on NSSF loans is administratively set, often higher than market — creates a debt trap for states
UPSC trap: NSSF is under the Union Government's Public Account — not included in budgetary borrowings directly, but lent out to governments
15th Finance Commission recommendation: states should reduce NSSF dependence and rely on market borrowings

concepts.name: Debt Relief and Restructuring: Paris Club, HIPC Initiative, and India's Creditor Role
key_dimensions: Paris Club: informal group of creditor nations that restructures sovereign debt — India joined as a participant, not just a debtor
HIPC (Heavily Indebted Poor Countries) Initiative: IMF-World Bank debt relief for eligible low-income countries — India benefited historically, now a creditor
India as a bilateral creditor: loans to Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, African nations under Lines of Credit — creates reciprocal debt management obligations
UPSC trap: IMF lending is NOT debt relief — it is conditional balance of payments support at concessional rates; HIPC is separate
G20 Common Framework for debt treatment: post-COVID initiative India actively participates in as G20 presidency holder (2023)

concepts.name: Ponzi Dynamics in Public Debt: Primary Deficit, r > g Condition, and Debt Trap
key_dimensions: Domar condition for debt sustainability: if nominal GDP growth rate (g) > nominal interest rate (r), debt-to-GDP ratio is self-stabilising
r > g condition: when borrowing cost exceeds growth rate, each period's primary surplus required to stabilise debt grows — debt trap risk
India's situation: historically g > r due to financial repression (SLR, administered rates) — this advantage is eroding with market-linked rates
Ponzi financing: government borrows only to pay interest — not rolling over productive debt but purely financing past interest — unsustainable
UPSC trap: primary surplus (not fiscal surplus) is the relevant variable for debt stabilisation — distinction between primary and overall balance is critical

concepts.name: Capital Account Convertibility and Its Link to External Debt Vulnerability
key_dimensions: Full capital account convertibility (CAC) would allow free flow of debt capital — India maintains partial CAC by design
Tarapore Committee I (1997) and II (2006): preconditions for CAC — fiscal consolidation, low inflation, strong banking sector
UPSC trap: Current account is fully convertible in India; capital account is only partially convertible — these are frequently confused
Sudden stop problem: if foreign investors can freely exit (full CAC), external debt rollover risk spikes during global risk-off episodes
FPI limits in G-Sec market (currently ~6% of outstanding stock): a macroprudential tool to limit external debt-linked capital account vulnerability

concepts.name: Centre-State Debt Relations: Loans from Centre, ORT Recommendations, and Fiscal Federalism
key_dimensions: Centre lends to states from NSSF and also on-lends external borrowings (World Bank, ADB loans) — states cannot directly access multilateral funds
UPSC trap: States cannot borrow externally — all multilateral loans are contracted by Centre and on-lent to states at a spread
Finance Commission's role: Article 293(3) requires states to obtain Centre's consent for loans if they are already indebted to Centre — leverage tool
Debt Consolidation and Relief Facility (DCRF) under 12th Finance Commission: consolidated and rescheduled state debt to Centre
15th Finance Commission: linked state borrowing limits to performance on power sector reforms, ease of doing business — conditional borrowing space
